investment_summary:
ASML's FY2025 20-F shows strong momentum: net sales rose 15.6% to €32.7bn, the operating margin widened to 34.6%, and diluted EPS rose to €24.71 from €19.24 [1]. EUV sales grew 39.4% while lithography unit shipments fell to 327 from 418 [1]. Operating cash flow of €12.7bn was flattered by €6.2bn of receivables factoring [1].

Consensus, dated after the 10-K, expects FY2026 revenue growth of 36.2% and FY2027 growth of 29.0%, with EPS estimates up 8.8% over 90 days [3]. The reverse DCF implies 20.1% annual revenue growth for ten years, above the 15.6% historical rate, and an implied return of 10.9% against an 11.5% WACC [2][3]. The price therefore requires growth well beyond history for a decade, even though near-term estimates are rising.

The main risks are concentration and policy: the largest customer is 23.9% of sales, and the export-control measures are suspended only until November 10, 2026 [1]. We view the shares as fully valued for the upside case rather than offering a margin of safety.
key_takeaways: Growth should hold as AI-driven EUV demand scales: net sales rose 15.6% to €32.7bn and EUV grew 39.4% [1].
Cash generation is strong, but €6.2bn of receivables factoring flatters operating cash flow, so quality is below the headline [1].
Consensus expects 36.2% growth in FY2026, which we think is too high versus management's €34–39bn guidance [1][3].
The shares need about 20% annual revenue growth for a decade to earn the WACC, leaving little margin of safety [2][3].
business_overview:
ASML Holding N.V. is a Dutch semiconductor equipment maker, founded in 1984, that supplies lithography, metrology and inspection systems, software and services to microchip manufacturers [1]. It reports one segment. Net sales reached €32.7bn in 2025, up 15.6% from €28.3bn, with net system sales of €24.5bn (up 12.4%) and net service and field option sales of €8.2bn (up 26.2%), which now make up 25.1% of sales against 23.0% a year earlier [1]. The product mix shifted toward advanced tools: EUV sales rose 39.4% to €11,602.7 million, with NXE at €10,445.8 million and EXE at €1,156.9 million, while ArF immersion grew 6.7% to €10.3bn and metrology and inspection rose 27.8% to €0.8bn [1]. Older DUV lines fell sharply, with KrF down 49.7% to €1.0bn [1].

Demand is driven by AI. The filing links the growth to advanced Logic and DRAM investment for AI infrastructure, and management expects the semiconductor market to grow at a 9% CAGR from 2025 to 2030 [1]. The installed base supports the service line, which management expects to keep growing in 2026 [1]. The company also depends on partners it does not fully control. Carl Zeiss SMT, in which ASML holds a 24.9% equity interest, is the sole supplier of critical optical components and paid ASML a €320.5m dividend in 2025, while in September 2025 ASML invested €1.3bn in Mistral AI for an 11.1% fully diluted stake [1].

Capital allocation has been shareholder-friendly. ASML returned €8.5bn in 2025, including €5.95bn of buybacks, and proposed a dividend of €7.50 per share, up 17.2% [1]. In January 2026 it announced buybacks of up to €12bn through 2028, while €1.7bn of debt principal falls due in 2026, so distributions depend on continued cash generation [1]. Shares outstanding fell 2.0% year on year to 385.4 million [2]. Consensus rates the stock Buy, with a mean target of $2,103.47 per share against a reference price of $1,256.41, both dated after the 10-K [3].
market_position:
ASML sits at the top of the advanced lithography supply chain. The filing gives no market share figure, so the leadership classification rests on sales mix and margin evidence rather than a disclosed share [1]. Its EUV line grew 39.4% while lithography unit shipments fell to 327 from 418, which the filing ties to lower volumes of older DUV tools, and EUV and immersion systems gained value share [1]. Gross margin of 52.8% trails only KLA's 60.9% among the three chosen peers [4].

Geography and customers show concentration. China (€9.5bn, 29.1% of sales) remained the largest market in 2025 but fell from 36.1% in 2024. Taiwan rose to 25.5% from 15.4%, South Korea to 25.0% from 22.7%, and the US contributed €4.1bn [1]. Four customers each exceeded 10% of sales, together €20.0bn or 61.2%, and the largest rose to 23.9% (€7.8bn) from 16.6% [1]. The filing does not name these customers. Logic net sales rose about €2.9bn on leading-edge foundry growth for AI, while Memory sales fell about €0.2bn after a strong 2024 [1]. The regional shift matters for the outlook, because it moves exposure away from a single policy-sensitive market.

Competition is intense in DUV and patterning, and the filing names Canon, Nikon, Applied Materials and KLA as rivals [1]. Analysts rate the shares Buy with a mean target about 67% above the reference price of $1,256.41, but the target range is wide, from $847.45 to $2,783.84 [3]. Consensus expects FY2026 revenue growth of 36.2%, far above management's €34–39bn guidance [1][3]. Positioning is therefore strong but exposed: a few buyers drive most sales, and the 2026 recovery in Logic and Memory capacity spending will decide whether the growth case holds [1].
operating_results:
ASML's 2025 operating results show revenue growth with better margins. Net sales rose 15.6% to €32.7bn from €28.3bn, driven by service and field option sales, which grew 26.2% to €8.2bn, and by EUV, while system sales rose 12.4% to €24.5bn even as units fell to 535 from 583 [1]. Cost of sales increased 11.9% to €15.4bn, below the rate of sales growth, which lifted gross margin to 52.8% from 51.3% [1]. Research and development rose 9.2% to €4.7bn and selling, general and administrative costs rose 7.9% to €1.3bn, so operating margin expanded to 34.6% from 31.9% [1]. Operating expenses therefore grew more slowly than sales, and that operating leverage reached the bottom line. Service carries a derived gross margin of about 50.9% against 48.2% a year earlier, so the mix shift toward installed-base revenue supported profitability (illustrative calculation from the filing's cost and sales lines) [1].

Net income rose 26.9% to €9.6bn, and the net margin widened to 29.4% from 26.8% [1]. Diluted EPS increased 28.4% to €24.71 from €19.24, helped by a lower diluted share count of 388.9m compared with 393.6m [1]. Tax expense rose 19.8%, which trims the benefit of higher pre-tax profit. Carl Zeiss SMT, the equity-accounted optics supplier, contributed €216.7m of profit, up from €209.8m [1]. Shares outstanding fell 2.0% year on year, which supports per-share growth [2].

The quality of the earnings needs care. Receivables factoring reached €6.2bn, against €2.0bn in 2024, which supports operating cash flow of €12.7bn and free cash flow of €11.0bn, but it brings cash forward rather than creating it [1]. Current deferred revenue rose to €16.0bn, which means customer prepayments are funding part of the growth. Management is therefore reporting growth that depends on advance payments, and investors should track whether deferred revenue converts into recognised sales in 2026. The 2026 guidance of €34–39bn implies growth of about 4–19%, a slower pace than 2025 [1]. Compared with the three peers, ASML's operating profile is strong: its 52.8% gross margin is above Applied Materials (48.7%) and Lam Research (48.7%) but below KLA (60.9%) [4].
risk_assessment:
ASML's risk profile is dominated by three exposures identified in the filing [1]. The first is customer concentration. The largest customer rose to 23.9% of net sales (€7.8bn) from 16.6% (€4.7bn), the two largest accounted for 38.0%, and lithography unit shipments fell from 418 to 327 [1]. Credit exposure follows the same pattern: the three largest customers held 35.4% of receivables at year-end 2025, down from 54.1%, but the filing warns that the insolvency of one main customer could cause significant credit losses [1]. Management also says costs are hard to adjust quickly after the company expanded its organisation, so a sharp downturn would press on margins [1].

The second is export controls and geopolitics. Dutch and US rules require licences for EUV systems and certain DUV immersion tools, and ASML does not control licensing decisions or the restricted list, which may expand [1]. China's share of sales fell to 29.1% from 36.1%, while Taiwan rose to 25.5% from 15.4%, and the filing highlights Taiwan's political status as a concentration risk [1]. The export-control measures are suspended until November 10, 2026, so the policy risk is time-bound and could return [1]. The third is supply concentration. Carl Zeiss SMT is the sole supplier of critical optics, system output is capped by its capacity, and all manufacturing takes place at eight facilities across the Netherlands, Germany, the US, South Korea and Taiwan [1].

Financial indicators provide some offset. Quality scores calculated from the financial statements put the Piotroski F-score at 8 of 9, the Altman Z-score at 10.61 in the safe zone, and the Beneish M-score at -3.01, well below the manipulation threshold, so there is no accounting warning sign [2]. The balance sheet is ample: cash and short-term investments of €13.3bn exceed total debt of €4.4bn [1][2]. However, the current ratio fell to 1.26x from 1.53x as deferred revenue rose to €16.0bn [1]. Latest-quarter liquidity data is dated after the 10-K and should be read as a later update. The thesis risk is that a demand slowdown would hit a cost base that is hard to shrink, while a policy shift or supplier disruption could remove volume at the same time.
competitors_analysis:
We chose Applied Materials (AMAT), Lam Research (LRCX) and KLA (KLAC) as peers. The filing names Applied Materials and KLA as competitors, and all three are US-listed wafer-equipment makers with similar capital-spending exposure. Lam Research is the closest process-equipment peer, KLA is the closest on the process-control and inspection side of ASML's metrology business, and the three are the most comparable US-listed names by business model and size, with revenue between 0.4x and 0.9x of ASML's [1][4]. ASML was the largest company in the group by 2025 revenue [4].

On growth, ASML's 15.6% in 2025 trailed Lam Research (23.7%) and KLA (23.9%) and was well ahead of Applied Materials (4.4%) [4]. Its profitability was second only to KLA: EBITDA margin was 38.4%, against 35.2% at Applied Materials, 35.4% at Lam Research and 43.9% at KLA, and ROIC was 39.5%, against 26.7%, 38.5% and 40.9% respectively [4]. Free cash flow conversion, measured as free cash flow to EBITDA, was 1.15 in 2025, the highest in the group [4]. ASML's gross margin of 52.8% sat between the peers' 48.7% and KLA's 60.9% [4].

The valuation gap is the main issue. ASML traded at 27.29x EV/EBITDA and 10.48x EV/Sales in 2025, against 18.51x and 6.51x at Applied Materials, 18.64x and 6.60x at Lam Research, and 22.89x and 10.06x at KLA [4]. Its trailing P/E of 36.53 compared with 26.92, 23.46 and 29.49 for the three peers [4]. The premium is not explained by growth, since two peers grew faster in 2025 at lower multiples. The 2026 peer multiples are much higher and the source does not show their basis, so they are excluded. Consensus puts ASML's forward EV/Sales at 9.7x for FY2026 and 7.5x for FY2027 [3]. ASML's advantage lies in margin and cash conversion; whether that justifies the premium depends on sustained growth, which consensus expects at 36.2% for 2026 [3]. This is the central test for the investment view.

investment_theses.invalidation: Gross margin falls below 50% in any 2026 quarter, or EPS misses consensus two quarters in a row [3].
